newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Higher oil prices hang over Spanish CPI.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Higher oil prices hang over Spanish CPI.

text.p: Spanish inflation, expected to decline steadily and break below three percent by the first quarter of 1997, could stagnate in October because of the recent rise in world oil prices, analysts said on Monday.
A Reuter poll of 16 financial experts showed that consumer prices could rise 0.2 percent month-on-month and 3.6 percent year-on-year. This compares with 0.2 and 3.6 in September.
October data are scheduled for release November 14.
"Right now the major risks for Spanish inflation are in oil prices, which showed a sharp rise," said Carmen Alcaide, economist at BBV in Madrid.
In October, 1996 Brent oil was around $24.1 a barrel compared with $22.6 in September, the highest price since February 1991, according to a publication by the Spanish oil producers association.
But as long as oil prices do not prompt substantial deviations from a declining trend, it should not bother the market, analysts said.
Earlier on Monday, speaking after the monthly G-10 central bankers meeting, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said oil prices had already reached their peak.
He added that future price movements will depend largely on such issues as the situation in Iraq and demand for oil.
"Also in the PPI energy was the most dynamic component," said Carmen Hernansanz at Merrill Lynch.
The Producer Price Index (PPI) rose in September a 0.3 percent month-on-month and 0.8 percent year-on-year, INE said earlier this morning.
In August it was unchanged and 0.8 percent respectively.
Core inflation -- which excludes energy and unprocessed food -- should confirm a downtrend, Alcaide said.
"If we forget the energy issue, core inflation's trend is a really good one," said Hernansanz.
"We are very positive on core inflation," she said, adding that they forecast it declining to 3.3 percent in October.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters forecast October core inflation at 0.3 percent and 3.6 percent after rises of 0.2 and 3.4 percent in September.

After recent remarks by officials in the Bank of Spain and Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government hinting at further declines in overall Spanish inflation, analysts said that CPI growth should decline below three percent by the first quarter of 1997.
Salomon Brother's economist Jose Luis Alzola said it is possible to reach something below three percent in January, while BBV forecast a decline beneath three percent in March.
With Spain pushing hard to find a place in the core countries of the European Monetary Union, the Bank of Spain is checking inflation closely before setting its monetary policy.
And at the end of October Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo said that any other rate cuts this year would depend by the inflation trend.
The Bank of Spain last cut its key money market rate, the repo, by 50 basis points to 6.75 percent on October 3.
